title: The horse is handsome, not you
hookLine: don't boast about your fine horse, as if its beauty were yours (Enchiridion 6)

lines: THE MAN WITH THE BEAUTIFUL HORSE.
cards: A man pulls into a parking lot in a very shiny car and takes a little longer than necessary to get out of it. A parent mentions, for the third time at dinner, which college the kid got into.
A fan says we won last night, about a team he has never played for. Each one is standing next to something fine and letting a little of its shine land on them.
Epictetus noticed it in the ancient equivalent: the man with the beautiful horse.

teach.b: Section six of the handbook says: don't be lifted up by an excellence that isn't yours. Then comes the joke.

teach.h: IF THE HORSE SAID I AM BEAUTIFUL.
teach.b: If the horse itself were proud, Epictetus says, and announced, I am beautiful, that would be bearable; the horse is, after all, beautiful.
But when you say, I have a beautiful horse, and puff up, you're proud of the horse's good, not yours. The mane, the speed, the gleam belong to the animal. You're just the one holding the rope.
So what is yours? His answer is a short phrase: the use of impressions. Every moment, things appear to you, a horse, an insult, a compliment, a fear.
What you do with those appearances, how you judge them and respond, that's yours.
When you handle them well, in line with nature, he says, then go ahead and be glad, because you're glad about a good that's really your own.
Why it matters on a Tuesday: borrowed pride is fragile. The car gets scratched. The team loses.

The kid has a hard year, and suddenly your sense of yourself wobbles along with theirs. Epictetus isn't saying don't enjoy the horse, or don't love the kid, or don't cheer. He's saying keep the accounts straight.
The horse is handsome. Your part is what you did today with what showed up, and that can't be scratched in a parking lot.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism notice when they take credit for something they merely own or stand near, and remind themselves that their own part is how they respond.

games.q: what does “the horse is handsome” mean?
o: the shine belongs to the thing, not to its owner
a Greek proverb praising a well-bred horse
a compliment you pay to win someone's favor

games.q: the horse is handsome — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says it would be bearable if the horse itself were proud
the horse really is beautiful; it's the owner's pride that's borrowed.
section six says don't enjoy owning a fine horse
it says don't be lifted up as if the horse's beauty were yours.
for Epictetus, what's truly yours is the use of impressions
how you judge and respond to what appears.

games.q: someone admires your beautiful horse. what does Epictetus have you notice?
o: that you chose well, so the credit is yours.
that the beauty belongs to the horse.
that you should sell it before it ages.
games.why: the excellence is the horse's. be glad about your own good: how you handle what appears to you.

practice: Think of one thing you feel a little proud of that isn't strictly yours, a possession, a title, where you went to school, a well-known relative, a city, a team, and give the credit back: the horse is handsome, with the real name in place of horse.
Notice whether anything in you shrinks or relaxes. Then ask what you actually did this week that was yours, and let one small answer come.

wordCard.voice: The horse is handsome. Epictetus' reminder that the shine of what we own or stand near belongs to it, not to us; ours is how we meet things. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the horse is handsome. The shine is the horse's; yours is how you meet what shows up. Day three hundred thirty-eight.
